content: Each year, tuberculosis (TB) claims the lives of approximately six million people, with the majority of these deaths occurring in developing countries. On March 24, 1882, Dr. Robert Koch made a groundbreaking announcement that revolutionized the understanding of TB. He revealed his discovery of the TB bacillus, the bacterium responsible for causing tuberculosis, which astonished the scientific community at the time. During the period of Dr. Koch's announcement in Berlin, tuberculosis was a devastating epidemic across Europe and the Americas, accounting for the death of one in every seven individuals. Dr. Koch's discovery marked a pivotal moment in medical history, as it paved the way for the development of diagnostic methods and treatments for TB. In 1982, on the centennial anniversary of Dr. Koch's historic presentation, the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (IUATLD) proposed that March 24 be officially recognized as World TB Day. Later, in 1996, the World Health Organization (WHO) collaborated with the IUATLD and numerous other organizations to amplify the global impact of World TB Day and raise awareness about the disease. In South Africa, the incidence of tuberculosis has tripled in recent years. This alarming increase is closely linked to the country's high prevalence of HIV infections, which complicates the management and treatment of TB. South African patients undergoing the six-month TB treatment regimen are eligible to receive a grant during this period. However, there are instances where treatment is intentionally interrupted in order to prolong eligibility for the grant, further exacerbating the challenges in controlling the disease.
